Learning Objectives
Describe the appearance of congenital vertical talus on physical examination and radiographs.
Recognize the association between congenital vertical talus and neuromuscular conditions and
genetic syndromes.
Understand the pathoanatomy of congenital vertical talus.
Differentiate congenital vertical talus from oblique talus, positional calcaneovalgus foot,
posteromedial bowing of the tibia, and clubfoot.
Review treatment strategies for patients with congenital vertical talus.

Rare, rigid rocker-bottom flatfoot deformity present at birth
Characterized by fixed dorsolateral dislocation of the navicular on the talar neck, calcaneal
equinovalgus, and contractures of the Achilles and peroneal tendons
Approximately 50% associated with underlying neuromuscular conditions or genetic
syndromes

Overview
Congenital vertical talus (CVT) is a rare congenital flatfoot deformity present at birth as a
rigid rocker-bottom arch. The deformity is produced by a fixed dorsolateral dislocation of
the navicular on the talar neck, calcaneal equinovalgus, and contractures of the Achilles
and peroneal tendons. The forefoot is dorsiflexed and abducted. The talus is
plantarflexed in a vertical position, and the talar head is palpable on the plantarmedial
aspect of the foot. A variable degree of calcaneocuboid joint subluxation or dislocation
may be present. Unmanaged CVT is associated with poor long-term outcomes and may
lead to foot and ankle pain, weak push-off strength, medial plantar sores or calluses, and
difficulty with shoe wear1,2 (Resources 1 and 2).
Epidemiology
Estimated incidence 1 in 10,000 live births
50% bilateral
No sex predilection

Epidemiology
Because of the rarity and lack of recognition of CVT in newborns, the exact incidence is
unknown, and large multicenter studies are necessary to obtain this information3,4
(Resources 3 and 4).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The navicular is hypoplastic and wedge-shaped.
The talar head is flattened superiorly and ovoid in length.
The calcaneus is displaced posterolaterally relative to the talus and tilted into equinus.
Overall, the medial column is elongated, whereas the lateral column is shortened.
Vascular Anatomy
The vascular supply may be dominated by the anterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries,
whereas the posterior tibial artery may be deficient; however, this pathoanatomy has not been
observed consistently.
Tendons
The Achilles, tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis brevis and longus,
and peroneus tertius tendons are contracted.
The posterior tibial and peroneal tendons may be displaced anteriorly over the medial and
lateral malleolus, respectively, such that they function as dorsiflexors rather than plantar
flexors.
Joints and Ligaments
The talonavicular joint is dislocated, with the navicular articulating with the dorsolateral aspect
of the talar neck.
Ligamentous abnormalities mirror bony deformities: the calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament is
attenuated and the tibionavicular portion of the superficial deltoid ligament is contracted,
thereby trapping the navicular in a dislocated position.
The dorsal aspect of the talonavicular capsule is contracted.
Musculature
Bones and joints:
The talonavicular joint is dislocated such that the navicular articulates with the dorsolateral
aspect of the talar neck. This locks the talus in a vertical position. The calcaneus is in equinus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Congenital Vertical Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000031
3/24

and valgus. A variable degree of calcaneocuboid joint subluxation may be present. The
corresponding talonavicular, posterior ankle, and subtalar joint capsules are contracted.
Ligaments:
The calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament is attenuated. The tibionavicular portion of the
superficial deltoid ligament is contracted, which keeps the navicular dislocated.
Muscles and tendons:
The hindfoot is in equinovalgus because of contractures of the Achilles and peroneal
tendons. The forefoot is abducted and dorsiflexed because of contractures of the tibialis
anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis brevis and longus, and peroneus
tertius tendons. The posterior tibial and peroneal tendons may be displaced anteriorly over
the medial and lateral malleolus, respectively, such that they function as dorsiflexors rather
than plantar flexors.
Etiology
Exact etiology unknown
Associated conditions
Approximately 50% of cases are associated with central nervous system, neuromuscular, or
genetic disorders, whereas the remaining 50% are isolated cases. Associated conditions
include myelomeningocele, arthrogryposis, and chromosomal abnormalities.
Genetics
Approximately 20% of isolated cases are autosomal dominant.
Mutations in HOX10 and GDF5 genes have been identified in some isolated cases.

Etiology
The exact etiology of CVT remains unknown. Approximately 50% of cases are associated
with central nervous system, neuromuscular, or genetic disorders, whereas the
remaining are isolated. The condition has been observed in approximately 10% of
patients with arthrogryposis and myelomeningocele. Other associated neurologic
disorders include neurofibromatosis and spinal muscular atrophy. The condition also
has been associated with prune belly, De Barsy, Costello, Rasmussen, split hand/foot,
and multiple pterygium syndromes. Aneuploidy of chromosomes 13, 15, and 18 also has
been associated with CVT.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Congenital Vertical Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000031
4/24

Approximately 20% of patients with isolated CVT have a positive family history, and the
most common inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant. Specific gene mutations
in HOX10 and GDF5 (also known as CDMP1) have been described in some isolated cases;
however, no single genetic abnormality has been associated with all cases.
The deformity may be the result of an arrest in fetal foot development between weeks
seven and twelve of gestation. Intrauterine malpositioning or molding may play a role
because CVT has been associated with congenital hip dislocation and contralateral
clubfoot.
Abnormalities of skeletal muscle have been correlated with CVT. Muscle biopsies have
revealed abnormal variation in fiber size, abnormal fiber type predominance, and
decreased size of type I fibers. Muscle imbalance in patients with central nervous system
or neuromuscular disorders, such as overpull of the anterior tibial tendon or weakness
of foot intrinsic muscles, also has been theorized as a potential cause.
Some studies have found a strong correlation between CVT and an absent posterior
tibial artery. However, an absent anterior tibial artery and a normal arterial supply also
have been described, suggesting that vascular deficiencies alone are not sufficient to
cause CVT4-6 (Resource 5).
Natural History
Gradual progression from painless deformity at birth to foot and ankle pain and gait
abnormalities

Natural History
Missed or neglected CVT may present in a delayed fashion with pain and difficulty with
ambulation and shoe wear. Painful sores and calluses may develop over the medial
aspect of the foot around the prominent and dislocated talar head. The normal rockers
of gait during the stance phase (ie, heel, ankle, and forefoot) are absent. Neglected CVT

deformity. (Images courtesy of Michael M. Chau, MD, PhD, Minneapolis, MN, and Jennifer

Classification
Coleman et al
Type I: rigid dorsal dislocation of the talonavicular joint

Type II: type I plus subluxation or dislocation of the calcaneocuboid joint
Lichtblau
Group I (teratogenic): inherited, presents with a very rigid deformity, often bilateral
Group II (neurogenic): result of muscular imbalance, the foot is more supple than the
teratogenic type
Group III (acquired): the result intrauterine malpositioning, deformity is partially correctable,
may be associated with other intrauterine packing disorders

Classification
Current classification systems for CVT are limited in their ability to guide management.
Some classification systems define oblique talus as a milder form of CVT. Other
classification systems focus on whether the condition is isolated or associated with
neurologic disorders.5
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Typically diagnosed at birth

Patient History
CVT typically is diagnosed at birth; however, it may be diagnosed on prenatal
ultrasonography. If observed prenatally, additional workup to evaluate for additional
anomalies usually is warranted.7
Physical Examination
Recognizable at birth
Initially painless and does not delay walking if missed or neglected
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000031
8/24

Convex plantar surface, the apex of which is the talar head, which results in a rocker-bottom
appearance and deep creases over the dorsum of the foot
The navicular is palpable because it lies on the dorsal aspect of the talar neck.
Contracted Achilles and tibialis anterior tendons, displaced peroneal and posterior tibialis
tendons, and taut posterolateral ligaments resist passive correction of the talonavicular joint.

Physical Examination
CVT is noticeable in newborns as a severe flatfoot deformity. The plantar aspect of the
foot is convex with a characteristic rocker-bottom appearance. The dislocated head of
the talus can be palpated on the medial aspect of the foot, and a palpable gap is noted
dorsally where the talonavicular articulation normally is located. The deformity has a
degree of flexibility if the dorsal gap reduces with forefoot plantar flexion. Deep skin
creases are present along the dorsum of the foot secondary to substantial forefoot and
midfoot dorsiflexion. The hindfoot is in equinovalgus (Figure 3).
A comprehensive physical examination is essential because of the frequency of genetic
and neuromuscular abnormalities associated with CVT. Facial dysmorphic features may
suggest a syndromic diagnosis, whereas a sacral dimple would be concerning for a
possible neuroaxis abnormality.
Figure 3 Clinical photographs of the feet of a newborn show the features of vertical
talus. The plantar aspects of the feet (A) show forefoot abduction deformities, and the
dorsolateral aspects of the feet (B) demonstrate deep creases on presentation
secondary to forefoot and midfoot dorsiflexion. (Reproduced with permission from

Orthop Surg 2015;23[10]:604-611.) 
Imaging Studies
Radiography
AP and three lateral views, standing views in older children
Neutral lateral view
The navicular is dislocated dorsally on the talar neck.
The talus appears nearly vertical in relation to the first metatarsal (increased talar axis–first
metatarsal base angle) and parallel to the tibia.
The calcaneus is in equinus (increased talocalcaneal and tibiocalcaneal angles).
Maximal plantar flexion lateral view
Persistent vertical orientation of the talus
In oblique talus, the talonavicular joint will reduce.
Maximal dorsiflexion lateral view
Persistent hindfoot equinus
In calcaneovalgus foot, the hindfoot is dorsiflexed and, therefore, not in equinus.
AP view
Increased talocalcaneal angle
Increased talar axis–first metatarsal angle
Ossification
The hindfoot and metatarsals are ossified at birth, the cuboid is ossified during the first
month of life, the cuneiforms are ossified at 2 years, and the navicular is ossified at 3 years.
In children younger than 3 years, the position of the navicular may be inferred from the
direction of the metatarsals or the position of the cuneiforms.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Spine MRI if an associated neuroaxis abnormality is suspected
Ultrasonography

Dynamic views may differentiate between vertical and oblique talus if radiography is equivocal
by identifying the unossified navicular and talar head.
In some patients, CVT is diagnosed prenatally via ultrasonography.

Ultrasonography
Standard radiographs for CVT include an AP view and three lateral views of the foot (in
neutral, maximal plantar flexion, and maximal dorsiflexion). The AP radiograph
demonstrates increased talocalcaneal and talar axis–first metatarsal angles. On lateral
radiographs, the long axis of the talus is vertically oriented relative to the first metatarsal
because of dorsal dislocation of the navicular. The talonavicular dislocation results in
high talocalcaneal and lateral talar axis–first metatarsal base angles; values greater than
35° are diagnostic of CVT. The calcaneus is in equinus, resulting in an elevated
tibiocalcaneal angle (Figure 4).

Figure 4 A, Lateral radiograph of the plantarflexed left foot of the patient shown in
Figure 3 demonstrates the fixed vertical position of the talus (line), with no reduction of
the midfoot on the hindfoot. B, Lateral radiograph of a plantarflexed foot with congenital
vertical talus demonstrates measurement of the lateral talar axis–first metatarsal base
angle (3), the lateral talocalcaneal angle (4), and the lateral tibiocalcaneal angle (5). C, AP
radiograph of a foot with congenital vertical talus demonstrates the measurement of the
AP talocalcaneal angle (1) and the AP talar axis–first metatarsal angle (2). (Reproduced
with permission from Miller M, Dobbs MB: Congenital vertical talus: Etiology and
management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2015;23[10]:604-611.)
The rigid deformity in CVT is irreducible compared with the flexible deformities of
oblique talus and positional calcaneovalgus feet. Maximum plantar flexion of the
forefoot will not reduce the dislocated talonavicular joint or correct the vertical
orientation of the talus in CVT. Similarly, maximum dorsiflexion will not correct the
hindfoot equinus (Figure 5). Conversely, maximum plantar flexion of the forefoot will
reduce the talonavicular joint in oblique talus.
In children younger than 3 years, the navicular is not ossified, and its position may be
inferred from the direction of the first metatarsal or the position of the cuneiforms. The
first metatarsal can be identified because its base is relatively distal and broad compared
with the other metatarsals. The hindfoot and metatarsals ossify at birth, the cuboid
ossify during the first month of life, the cuneiforms ossify at 2 years, and the navicular
ossify at 3 years. Dynamic ultrasonography may assist in differentiating CVT from
oblique talus if radiography is equivocal by identifying the unossified navicular and talar
head.
MRI of the spine may be indicated if the patient history and physical examination
findings suggest an associated central nervous system pathology4,8 (Resource 6).

Differential Diagnosis
Oblique talus: flexible subluxation of the talonavicular joint
Positional calcaneovalgus foot: hindfoot eversion and dorsiflexion resulting from soft-tissue
contractures and intrauterine positioning
Posteromedial bowing of the tibia: idiopathic deformity and growth inhibition of the tibia,
associated with calcaneovalgus foot
Clubfoot: idiopathic or teratologic cavus, forefoot adductus, hindfoot varus, equinus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM

13/24


Differential Diagnosis
Oblique talus may be classified as a milder form of CVT on a spectrum of severity. It is
differentiated by talonavicular joint subluxation that is passively correctable with
maximum forefoot plantar flexion (Figure 6). Oblique talus typically responds to
observation or cast immobilization alone; however, some surgeons will manage an
oblique talus as a CVT if it is accompanied by Achilles tendon contracture.
Figure 6 Lateral radiographs of the foot of a 3-month-old boy with an oblique talus
demonstrate a reducible talonavicular joint. In neutral flexion (A) and plantar flexion (B),
the lateral talar axis–first metatarsal base angle corrects from approximately 75° to 30°
with maximum plantar flexion. (Images courtesy of Michael M. Chau, MD, PhD,
Minneapolis, MN, and Jennifer C. Laine, MD, Saint Paul, MN.)
Positional calcaneovalgus foot, as the name suggests, is a flexible deformity caused by
soft-tissue contractures. In contrast to CVT, the hindfoot is in dorsiflexion rather than
equinus, and the plantar aspect of the foot is flat rather than convex. Management
typically consists of observation; stretching; or, occasionally, cast immobilization.
Posteromedial bowing of the tibia is an idiopathic deformity and growth inhibition that
may be confused with CVT because of similar clinical appearance of a calcaneovalgus
foot. Radiographs showing the apex of the deformity in the tibia are diagnostic (Figure
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Congenital Vertical Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000031
14/24

7). Management typically consists of observation. Epiphysiodesis may be indicated for
residual leg-length discrepancy.
Although CVT and clubfoot are associated with very different clinical and radiographic
appearances, many congenital foot anomalies are mislabeled as clubfoot. Although
patients with CVT and patients with clubfoot have equinus, the foot positions are
otherwise quite different: severe planus versus cavus, forefoot abduction versus
adduction, and hindfoot valgus versus varus, respectively. Surgeons should be able to
easily differentiate between the two conditions on clinical examination.4,5
Figure 7 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the lower extremity of an 11-day-old child
with posteromedial bowing of the tibia. Although the ankle may clinically appear
dorsiflexed, the apex of the deformity is located at the tibia. The alignment between the
talus and the metatarsals is normal. (Images courtesy of Michael M. Chau, MD, PhD,
Minneapolis, MN, and Jennifer C. Laine, MD, Saint Paul, MN.)

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
First-line treatment in idiopathic and teratologic cases
Performed during infancy as soon as possible
Techniques/Procedures
Minimally invasive Dobbs method (also called reverse Ponseti method)
Serial manipulation and cast immobilization
After the talonavicular joint reduces, it is pinned to maintain reduction, a percutaneous
Achilles tenotomy is performed to correct the equinus contracture, and a final cast is placed.
Transition to brace or orthosis after the final cast is removed

Techniques/Procedures
The current standard of care for the management of CVT is minimally invasive. Serial
manipulation and cast immobilization, known as the Dobbs or reverse Ponseti method,
is performed as soon as possible in infants, similar to the Ponseti method for patients
with clubfoot. The forefoot is stretched into plantar flexion and inversion by applying
distal traction to the metatarsals as a counterforce is applied to the medial aspect of the
talar head (Figure 8). The calcaneus is pulled downward to stretch the equinus
deformity. The foot is immobilized in a cast in the most corrected position. After the
talonavicular joint reduces, which typically requires four to six casts changed weekly, it is
pinned to maintain reduction, a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy is performed to correct
the equinus contracture, and the foot is immobilized in a cast in neutral (Figure 9). The
foot is transitioned to a brace or orthosis after the final cast is removed 2 weeks
later.1,4,9

Surgical Management
Indications
Minimally invasive treatment options as part of the Dobbs method
Major surgical management is second-line treatment.
Techniques/Procedures
One-stage versus two-stage soft-tissue release
Navicular excision or subtalar arthrodesis in older children with recalcitrant deformities
Triple arthrodesis in symptomatic adolescents

Techniques/Procedures
Surgical treatment with soft-tissue releases in patients aged approximately 1 year was
the mainstay of management for CVT; however, such management has become second-
line treatment because of the potential complications of stiffness, inadequate correction,
osteonecrosis of the talus, and wound necrosis. Although patients with mild CVT require
less extensive releases, patients with rigid arthrogrypotic deformities may require
circumferential releases.
Surgical management can be performed via a one- or two-stage approach. The one-stage
approach is favored and can be performed via a posterior Cincinnati incision or a dorsal
incision. The first step is to reduce the talonavicular joint by releasing the anterior tibialis
tendon and the tibionavicular and talonavicular ligaments. This is followed by pinning
the talonavicular joint and reconstructing the spring ligament. The second step is to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Congenital Vertical Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000031
18/24

reduce the forefoot by lengthening the peroneal tendons and the toe extensors. The
calcaneocuboid joint is reduced, if necessary, by releasing the bifurcate ligament and the
calcaneocuboid joint capsule. The third step is to correct the equinus contracture by
lengthening the Achilles tendon and releasing the ankle and the subtalar joint capsules.
The fourth step is to dynamically stabilize the correction by transferring the anterior
tibialis tendon to the talus. Postoperative cast immobilization is recommended for 6 to
12 weeks.
In children older than 3 years with recalcitrant deformities, a naviculectomy may be
required to accomplish the first step of correction. In addition, a concomitant Grice-
Green extra-articular arthrodesis of the subtalar joint may be performed at the time of
surgical releases. Salvage procedures, such as a triple arthrodesis, are reserved for
symptomatic adolescent patients4,5,10 (Resource 7).
Complications
Missed or neglected diagnosis
Inadequate correction
Recurrent deformity
Residual midfoot sag and forefoot abduction
Scar formation because of extensive soft-tissue release resulting in pain and stiffness
Osteonecrosis of the talus
Wound necrosis
Progression of early degenerative joint disease

Complications
CVT may be missed or neglected. Deformity correction at a younger age (<27 months)
yields more predictable outcomes and may avoid the need for extensive soft-tissue
release or salvage procedures. Even with timely management, residual or recurrent
deformity and progression of early degenerative joint disease may occur. Complications
after surgical correction are not uncommon and may be severe. Under-correction or
overcorrection of the deformity is possible. Soft-tissue scar formation after surgical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Congenital Vertical Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000031
19/24

correction may lead to pain and stiffness of the ankle or subtalar joint. Osteonecrosis of
the talus has been described. One study reported wound necrosis because of
overstretching and compromising the dorsal arterial supply to the foot, resulting in
amputation.5,10,11
Outcomes
Recurrence of idiopathic CVT managed via a minimally invasive treatment option is uncommon
but more likely in patients older than 12 months.
Treatment outcomes in children older than 3 years are less predictable.
Patients with CVT associated with underlying neurologic syndromes can be effectively treated
via a minimally invasive treatment option.
Improved ankle range of motion, pain and functional scores, and radiographic parameters
after minimally invasive management compared with extensive soft-tissue release surgery
have been reported.

Outcomes
In a retrospective series of 35 patients (47 feet) with a mean age 12.8 months (range, 1
week to 60 months) who had idiopathic CVT and underwent minimally invasive
correction, radiographic recurrence of talonavicular deformity occurred in 4 feet (9%)
during a follow-up period of 45 months.12 No additional surgical treatment was
required. Patient age older than 12 months at the time of treatment was a substantial
risk factor for radiographic recurrence.
Unmanaged CVT is associated with poor outcomes. Long-term sequelae of CVT include
foot and ankle pain, weak push-off strength, medial plantar sores or calluses, and
difficulty with shoe wear. Delayed treatment in children older than 3 years is
considerably more difficult and less predictable.
In a retrospective study of 25 patients (40 feet) with a mean age of 20.7 months (range, 1
week to 68 months) who had syndromic CVT managed via a minimally invasive treatment
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:47 AM
AAOS | Congenital Vertical Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000031
20/24

option, radiographic recurrence of CVT was observed in 12 feet (30.9%) and corrective
surgical treatment was performed in 7 feet (15.6%).13 Mean follow-up was 55 months. A
higher recurrence rate was noted in patients with distal arthrogryposis.
A retrospective study of 27 patients treated for CVT via the Dobbs method versus
extensive soft-tissue release reported improved range of motion, pain and functional
scores, and radiographic parameters at a mean follow-up of 7 years in the patients who
underwent the Dobbs method (Figure 10). A prospective cohort of 21 feet with
idiopathic and teratologic CVT reported a recurrence rate of 48% (10 of 21 feet) with the
Dobbs method. The teratologic group tended to have higher risk for recurrence;
however, the rate of recurrence was less than that associated with extensive surgical
releases9,14,15 (Resource 8).
